title: The Hidden Profile
text:
Groups are supposed to be wiser than individuals partly because members bring different information to the table. In 1985, Garold Stasser and William Titus at Miami University in Ohio tested whether groups actually use that information.

Students met in groups of four to choose the best of three fictional candidates for student body president. Each candidate came with a list of facts. In some groups, everyone received the full list. In others, the facts were split in a clever way: the information everyone shared made a weaker candidate look best, while the facts that pointed to the strongest candidate were scattered, each held by only one member. If the group pooled everything, the best choice became clear. This setup became known as a hidden profile.

With full information, groups usually picked the best candidate. With the hidden profile, they rarely did. Discussion dwelt on facts that everyone already knew, because those came up more often and were confirmed by others. Facts held by a single member were mentioned less, repeated less, and often never entered the conversation at all. Members also tended to argue for the candidate they had favored before the meeting, using the shared facts to support it.
lesson: Meetings tend to recycle what everyone already knows. Before deciding, ask each person directly for what only they know, and write it down where all can see it.
source: Stasser, G., and Titus, W. (1985). Pooling of unshared information in group decision making: Biased information sampling during discussion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(6), 1467-1478.
